contributions.headingText:
The WHO Classification of Tumours series serves as a basis for diagnosis and treatment and forms a pillar of evidence-based medicine. Along with staging guidelines, it allows for the comparison of data generated in different centres through clinical trials to be interpretable. Without a uniform classification and staging, clinical trial results are not generalizable. The advances made through clinical trials have contributed to significant improvements in patient outcomes for many tumour types over the past 50 years {36633525}. Although the need for internationally recognized and accepted classification systems is easy to demonstrate, the basis of such systems is less obvious. The sixth edition of the WHO Classification of Tumours follows closely the fifth edition, and the decision to undertake an update at this time was based on the significant evolution in the evidential basis for tumour classification at all body sites.

A change in the sixth edition is that all non-neoplastic entities in the fifth edition have been removed and are now only mentioned in the introduction to the relevant chapters. This modification was implemented to reflect the primary purpose of a tumour classification system.

Most of the individual volumes in the WHO Classification of Tumours series remain organ-based; it has been recognized for centuries that cancers arising from different organs have different clinical characteristics. In the case of gynaecological pathology, even the site within an organ was recognized to be important very early on; carcinomas of the uterine corpus and uterine cervix arise in patients with different risk factors, and with the introduction of microscopy, they were recognized to be of different cell types. The subclassification of carcinomas of different organs based on cell type or histological type was the next major advance in tumour classification. The supremacy of organ/histological type–based classification was challenged only with the arrival of immunohistochemistry and nucleic acid–based molecular diagnostics. This happened at different times in different organ systems. Although lymphomas and breast carcinoma were classified based on molecular features decades ago, it was only with the fifth edition of the classification of Female genital tumours that the integrated morphological-molecular classification approach was embraced [[Lax SF, Cheung AN, Oliva El. General introduction. In: WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Female genital tumours. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2020. (WHO classification of tumours series, 5th ed.; vol. 4). https://publications.iarc.fr/592.]]. This trend towards incorporating both morphology and molecular diagnostics in female genital tumour classification continues in the sixth edition.

The organ site of origin, histological type, and molecular pathology are not independent. Both organ site and cell type show strong associations with molecular features. With regard to the former, squamous cell carcinoma of the ovary, arising from a teratoma; squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, arising secondary to oncogenic HPV; and squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva of HPV-independent type are not closely related and warrant classification as separate tumour types despite being of the same histological type. Histological type is, however, an important classifier, for example, in the ovary, where the five major histological types of ovarian carcinoma are associated with differences in risk factors, patterns of spread, response to chemotherapy, association with hereditary cancer susceptibility syndromes, and molecular pathology. The in-depth molecular interrogation of thousands of tumours of more than 30 types from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) demonstrated the importance of cell of origin and cell type as determinants of the underlying molecular pathology {29625048}. In the sixth edition of the Female genital tumours volume of the WHO Classification of Tumours series, therefore, the traditional overarching classification framework for epithelial neoplasms, incorporating site and cell type, is retained. There are some exceptions to this; for tumours that occur at more than one site but are indistinguishable at the different sites, such as intestinal-type adenocarcinomas of vulva and vagina or clear cell carcinoma of cervix and vagina, only one detailed discussion is provided (in section Tumours of the vagina, with reference made to that section in section Tumours of the vulva, for the former; in section Epithelial tumours of the uterine cervix, with reference to that section in the chapter on vagina, for the latter).

Although site and cell type are used as a basis for classification of the epithelial neoplasms, the mesenchymal, melanocytic, and haematolymphoid neoplasms are presented as single chapters spanning all sites in the female genital tract. While many such tumours occur preferentially in specific sites, and these are noted, the histopathological and molecular features are typically broadly similar at all sites.

An emerging challenge is those situations where there are immunohistochemical and molecular markers that are necessary for further subclassification, such as vulvar squamous cell carcinoma. Although there are morphological features that correlate with HPV-independent and HPV-associated vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, for example, the sensitivity and specificity of a purely morphological approach will lead to errors in classification. It is recommended that, where resources permit, classification into HPV-associated or HPV-independent types (using immunohistochemistry and/or molecular testing; in practice, in most institutions, this is likely to be performed with p16 immunohistochemistry) be done in all cases. In this edition, there has been attention to how classification can be applied in low-resource settings, so that the WHO classification can be used worldwide. This is necessarily done on a tumour-by-tumour basis, where appropriate. In the example above, i.e. vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, if p16 immunostaining is not available, a tumour can be classified as “squamous cell carcinoma, HPV status undetermined”. Wherever possible, the essential diagnostic criteria were crafted to both emphasize the time-honoured morphological approach to tumour classification and to acknowledge constraints in accessing ancillary diagnostic resources that exist in many areas of the world; as such, ancillary studies are generally not incorporated into the essential diagnostic criteria unless absolutely necessary.

The chapter on mesenchymal tumours has changed the most since the fifth edition. The former morphology-based classification, with most uterine sarcomas being leiomyosarcoma, endometrial stromal sarcoma (low- or high-grade), or undifferentiated sarcoma, does not adequately reflect the rapid evolution of our understanding of uterine mesenchymal neoplasms. Some entities can be diagnosed only on the basis of the presence of a specific molecular feature, such as SMARCA4- and SMARCB1-deficient uterine sarcoma and NTRK-rearranged sarcoma. This is an area that undoubtedly will continue to evolve rapidly.

In this sixth edition, we also encourage consistent terminology for reporting several important immunohistochemical markers. p53 immunohistochemical staining is used as a surrogate marker of an underlying TP53 mutation; it is important to realize that while this is a good surrogate marker, it is not perfect. There are various terminologies applied in reporting p53 immunohistochemical staining, and it is stressed that this should not be reported as positive or negative. Terms such as “mutation-type”, “wildtype”, “aberrant”, “abnormal”, and “normal” are often used. In this sixth edition, we have used the terms “mutation-type” and “wildtype” throughout. The former is the type of p53 staining that is suggestive of an underlying TP53 mutation, and there are three patterns (diffuse strong positive staining in ≥ 80% of cells, completely negative [null-type] with a positive internal control, and cytoplasmic staining); the different patterns are associated with different types of TP53 mutation, although the association is not perfect {29517499; 27840695; 31829441; 33899789}. Wildtype staining is the pattern of staining that is not associated with an underlying TP53 mutation and is characterized by heterogeneous staining of variable intensity in cells, with some being negative and some being positive; wildtype staining may vary from near negative (can be confused with null-type) to so-called high wild type, which may be confused with diffuse mutation-type. In HPV-associated premalignant squamous lesions and squamous cell carcinomas, a mid-epithelial pattern of wildtype staining with basal sparing (distinct absence of staining in basal cells juxtaposed with strong staining in parabasal cells) has been described, which can also be confused with diffuse mutation-type immunoreactivity {32238876; 32203095}. Herein we consistently use the terms “mutation-type” and “wild type”, and when reporting the former we suggest elaborating on this by detailing the pattern. In a series of tubo-ovarian high-grade serous carcinomas with molecularly proven TP53 mutations, 66% of tumours exhibited diffuse mutation-type staining, 25% null mutation-type staining, and 4% cytoplasmic mutation-type staining {27840695}. Importantly, 5% of tumours exhibited wildtype immunoreactivity, illustrating that a TP53 mutation may occasionally be present even when there is wildtype immunohistochemical staining. Another important point to make is that before diagnosing null mutation-type staining, there should be a positive internal control with scattered nuclear staining of endothelial, stromal, and inflammatory cells. It should also be noted that p53 immunohistochemical staining is particularly prone to fixation issues and is often more reliable on biopsy than on resection specimens. Subclonal p53 immunohistochemical staining also occasionally occurs when some of the tumour exhibits wildtype and other areas exhibit mutation-type immunoreactivity. This may be secondary to a TP53 mutation occurring during tumour progression or associated with a hypermutated or ultramutated state, for example, underlying mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency or POLE mutation. If mutation-type p53 staining is subclonal, this should be clearly stated in the pathology report. In some tumour types, for example, ovarian mucinous tumours and vulvar squamous cell carcinomas, p53 staining may be more difficult to interpret due to the phenomenon of terminal differentiation where terminally differentiated cells fail to express p53 protein even in the presence of a TP53 mutation {32724153; 37500307; 32203095}.

Similarly, there are a few different terms that are commonly applied when reporting the results of p16 immunohistochemical staining, and a simple report of positive or negative is not appropriate. P16 is often used as a useful surrogate marker of a high-risk HPV-associated lesion in the appropriate morphological context {22742517}. The type of p16 staining associated with a high-risk HPV-associated lesion is often described as block-type and that is the terminology we employ herein. Block-type staining is characterized by diffuse strong nuclear (almost always with accompanying cytoplasmic) staining in virtually every cell. Although the term “block-type” was originally coined for squamous intraepithelial lesions (SILs) (discussed in section Squamous intraepithelial lesions), it is in widespread use for non-squamous lesions and carcinomas. Other terms used to describe block-type p16 staining include “aberrant” and “abnormal”. Patterns of p16 staining other than block-type are often referred to as non–block-type, mosaic, normal, negative, or non-aberrant. Herein, we recommend the term “negative/non–block-type”. It is emphasized that some other malignancies that are not associated with high-risk HPV may exhibit block-type p16 staining, for example, tubo-ovarian high-grade serous carcinomas, endometrial serous carcinomas, and (rarely) even some HPV-independent cervical adenocarcinomas {26685087}. It should also be recognized that neoplasms can exhibit diffuse strong p16 immunoreactivity without this being block-type; in cases such as this, isolated individual or small groups of cells will be negative, and this should not be mistaken for block-type immunoreactivity. Additionally, rarely high-risk HPV-associated neoplasms may be p16 negative or exhibit areas of block-type and negative staining. The latter is a rare scenario, and molecular HPV testing may be necessary to prove a high-risk HPV association {10535995}.

MMR immunoreactivity should also be reported using consistent and appropriate terminology and not as positive or negative {33290350}. In reporting MMR immunohistochemistry, “normal retained nuclear immunoreactivity” is the term that should be used for cases with intact staining. When there is loss of nuclear expression of one or more MMR proteins, the proteins that are lost should be specified. Before accepting loss of staining for any of the individual MMR proteins, a positive internal control should be identified with positive staining of endothelial, inflammatory, and stromal cells in the area where there is loss in the tumour cells. Occasionally, the loss of MMR protein expression may be subclonal (usually as a somatic event and sometimes in association with a POLE mutation, e.g. in an endometrial carcinoma); when subclonal loss of expression is present, this should be mentioned in the report and the protein(s) that exhibit loss of staining should be specified. As with p53 staining, MMR immunohistochemical staining is particularly prone to fixation issues and is often more reliable on biopsy than on resection specimens.
